subject: Cooking
title: You Don't Need 8 Glasses of Water a Day
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on You Don't Need 8 Glasses of Water a Day.

hook.text: Eight glasses of water a day — 64 ounces — is repeated everywhere. No scientific study supports this number.

buildup.text: The myth likely traces to a 1945 USDA report that mentioned 2.5 liters of water daily — including water in food.

discovery.text: About 20% of daily water intake comes from food — fruits, vegetables, soup, and even coffee contribute.

twist.text: Coffee and tea count toward hydration despite mild diuretic effects — the net fluid gain is positive.

climax.text: The best hydration indicator is urine color: pale yellow means you're fine. Thirst works too.

punchline.text: Your body already tells you when to drink. It's called thirst.

quiz.question: What's the best indicator of adequate hydration?

details.summary: The eight-glasses-a-day rule has no scientific basis. Hydration needs vary by body size, activity level, climate, and diet. Foods contain significant water, and thirst is a reliable indicator of hydration needs for most healthy people. Overhydration can actually be dangerous.
details.whyItMatters: This arbitrary number creates unnecessary anxiety about water intake. Trusting thirst signals and understanding that food provides water simplifies healthy hydration dramatically.
takeaways: The eight-glass rule has no documented scientific origin
About 20 percent of daily water comes from food consumption
Thirst is a reliable hydration guide for most healthy adults

faq.question: Where did the eight-glasses rule come from?
faq.answer: It likely originated from a 1945 US government recommendation that mentioned 2.5 liters of daily water, including water from food. People ignored the food part and converted it to eight 8-ounce glasses. No study has validated this specific number as optimal.

faq.question: Can you drink too much water?
faq.answer: Yes. Hyponatremia occurs when excessive water dilutes blood sodium to dangerous levels. It is rare but can be fatal, and has occurred in marathon runners and military training. For most people, drinking to satisfy thirst is sufficient and safe.
